8.title: start with the person in the mirror
8.hook: start with the person in the mirror
8.howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness (metta) meditation, practitioners often begin by silently wishing themselves well with a few short phrases, then extend the same wishes to a friend, a stranger, a difficult person and finally all beings.

screen: `DAY EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: thoughts. Your line: let it pass. Did one loud thought show up sounding very sure of itself? Did you let it pass, even once? Day eight, and week two begins.
screen: `THOUGHTS.` → `LET IT PASS.`

segments.voice: A friend burns the dinner. Misses a deadline. Says the wrong thing at the wrong moment. What comes out of your mouth? Usually something like: hey, it happens, you're tired, it's fine. Now flip it. You burn the dinner. What does the voice inside say then? Sometimes it's a voice nobody would be allowed to use on a friend. Idiot. Of course you did. Typical. Week two is about how we treat people. And one old tradition insists you start with the person in the mirror. Today's word is kindness.
screen: `WHAT YOU SAY TO A FRIEND.` → `WHAT YOU SAY TO YOURSELF.` → `START WITH THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: In the early Buddhist teachings there's a word, metta. It's usually translated loving-kindness, but it comes from the Pali word for friend. Metta is friendliness: wanting good for someone the way a friend does. A short discourse called the Metta Sutta describes it with a picture: the way a mother would protect her only child with her own life, a person can grow a heart like that toward every living being, without limit. Here's the surprise. The Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa wrote a long guide to meditation, the Path of Purification, and when he explains how to practice metta, he says not to start with everyone. Start with yourself. Wish yourself well first, with phrases like may I be happy, may I be free from trouble. Then extend it outward: to someone dear, to someone neutral, and eventually to someone difficult. His reasoning is plain. You know from the inside that you want to be happy. That makes you the example: everyone else wants the same. Remember day four, and the line from Leviticus: "love thy neighbour as thyself." Those last two words carry a quiet assumption, that there's some care for yourself to measure by. And modern research points somewhere similar. The psychologist Kristin Neff studies what she calls self-compassion: treating your own failures the way you'd treat a friend's. A common worry is that being kind to yourself will make you lazy. Some of this research points the other way: in one set of studies, people nudged to be gentler about a mistake were more willing to own it, and put more effort into doing better. Kindness isn't a reward for getting it right. It's where you start.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then picture yourself the way a good friend might see you right now: tired, trying, doing your best with the day you've had. On each breath out, say quietly inside: may I be at ease. That's all. If it feels strange or even a little silly, that's normal. Say it anyway. The bell holds the time.
Kindness. Wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with the one in the mirror. Eighth word.
screen: `KINDNESS — your 8th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: may I be at ease. Today, the next time you catch the harsh voice inside after a mistake, stop and ask what you'd say to a friend. Then say that to yourself. Day eight.

9.title: three things, out loud, badly
9.tomorrow: the thing every tradition's mystics agree on
9.howItsDone: Many people keep a short gratitude practice: a few things written in a notebook each night, a thanksgiving said at meals, or, in Jewish tradition, a brief prayer of thanks said on waking.

screen: `DAY NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: kindness. Your line: may I be at ease. When the harsh voice showed up, did you manage to answer it the way you'd answer a friend? Day nine.
screen: `KINDNESS.` → `MAY I BE AT EASE.`

segments.voice: Family dinner. Somebody says, okay, everyone name one thing you're thankful for. Half the table groans. Somebody says the food. Somebody says Wi-Fi. A kid says the dog. It's awkward, it's a bit forced, and it's over in a minute. That clumsy minute may be worth more than it looks. Today asks for three things. Out loud. Badly. Not eloquent, not a speech, not the perfect list. Just said. Today's word is gratitude.
screen: `NAME ONE THING.` → `THE FOOD, THE WI-FI, THE DOG.` → `THREE THINGS, OUT LOUD, BADLY.`

segments.voice: Start with an emperor. Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome, and kept a notebook we now call the Meditations, written, it seems, for himself. And the first book of it, as it comes down to us, isn't philosophy at all. It's a list of thank-yous. From his grandfather, good morals and an even temper. From his mother, generosity, and a simple way of living. Teacher after teacher, friend after friend, what each one gave him. A man who ruled an empire opens his notebook by counting what he'd been given. Now jump to the Christian letters of the New Testament. Paul, writing to a young church in Thessalonica, tells them, in the old King James wording: "In every thing give thanks." Notice he doesn't say for everything. In everything. Inside whatever is happening, find something to thank. Jewish tradition has a short prayer, the Modeh Ani, said on waking, while still in bed, thanking God for giving back the soul for another day. Thanks comes first, before coffee, before news. And then the lab. In 2003 the psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked some people to write down, each week, a few things they were grateful for, while others wrote about hassles or ordinary events. After ten weeks, the gratitude group rated their lives as a whole more highly and felt more hopeful about the week ahead. Nobody was asked to feel grateful first. They were only asked to write it down. That's why badly is allowed. Gratitude isn't a mood you wait for. It's a thing you say, and on hard days you say it anyway.

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and yes, it's out loud. If you're somewhere you can't speak, whisper it, or move your lips. Name three things you're thankful for right now. The first three that come. They can be tiny: warm socks, a text from someone, the fact that the bus came. Say them badly. Then, while the bell holds about forty-five seconds, sit with the third one and let it land. The bell holds the time.
Gratitude. Noticing what you've been given, and saying so, even when the feeling hasn't arrived yet. Ninth word.
screen: `GRATITUDE — your 9th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: thank you anyway. Today, when something goes a little wrong, find one small thing inside it to thank. Say it, even under your breath. Day nine.

10.title: the thing every tradition's mystics agree on
10.hook: the thing every tradition's mystics agree on
10.howItsDone: Silence is practiced in many forms: Quaker meetings for worship held in shared silence, silent retreats in Christian and Buddhist monasteries, and the Orthodox practice of stillness called hesychasm.

screen: `DAY TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: gratitude. Your line: thank you anyway. Did you find one small thing to thank inside something that went wrong? Day ten.
screen: `GRATITUDE.` → `THANK YOU ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: When was the last time you heard nothing? Not quiet with a podcast. Not quiet with the fridge humming and a phone buzzing in the next room. Nothing. It's easy to go a long time without it. The car, the shower, the walk to the shop all get filled. Here's something odd. The mystics of the world's traditions disagree about a great deal: God, the soul, what happens after death. But when you read what they actually did, one thing keeps showing up, from monasteries to meeting houses to mountain caves. They got quiet. Today's word is silence.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU LAST HEAR NOTHING?` → `THEY DISAGREE ABOUT A LOT.` → `AND THEY GOT QUIET.`

segments.voice: Start in the Hebrew Bible. The prophet Elijah is running for his life and hides in a cave on a mountain. A great wind comes, tearing rocks apart, but the text says God was not in the wind. Then an earthquake, and God was not in the earthquake. Then fire, and God was not in the fire. And then, in the King James wording, "after the fire a still small voice." That Hebrew phrase is hard to carry into English. It has also been rendered a gentle whisper, and a sound of thin silence. Either way, what comes after the noise is quiet. In the Psalms: "Be still, and know that I am God." In Eastern Orthodox Christianity, monks on Mount Athos in Greece are known for a way of prayer called hesychasm, named for a Greek word meaning stillness. In traditional Quaker meetings, Friends gather for worship by sitting together in silence, and speaking only when someone feels moved to. The early Buddhist discourses describe the Buddha telling monks that when they gather they should either talk about the teaching or keep what he called noble silence. In China, the Tao Te Ching puts it sharply: those who know don't talk about it, and those who talk about it don't know. Now, careful. These traditions don't agree about what's found in the silence. For some it's God. For some it's the mind seeing itself clearly. For some it's the Tao, which can't be named. Silence doesn't erase their differences. But it's a room each of these voices walks into. Quiet isn't the absence of the thing. For each of them, in its own way, quiet is where it is.
screen: `NOT THE WIND, NOT THE FIRE.` · `BE STILL, AND KNOW.` · `STILLNESS, MEETING, NOBLE SILENCE.` · `DIFFERENT THINGS FOUND IN THE SAME ROOM.` · then, large: `QUIET IS WHERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you can, turn off one sound near you: the music, the TV, the notifications. Then sit. For the next forty-five seconds, don't try to make the mind silent. Just listen to the silence that's already around the sounds. The hum, and the space around the hum. If you pray, you can hold a line from the Psalms: be still, and know. If you don't, just listen. The bell holds the time.
Silence. A room that prophets, monks, Friends and sages all walk into, even when they find different things there. Tenth word.
screen: `SILENCE — your 10th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: quiet is where it is. Today, pick one ordinary stretch, the drive, the dishes, the walk, and don't fill it. Let it stay quiet. Day ten.

screen: `DAY 10 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY SUNSET IS THE HOUR.`

11.title: why sunset is the hour
11.hook: why sunset is the hour; every culture stopped at dusk
11.tomorrow: Ram Dass: we're all just walking each other home
11.howItsDone: Several traditions mark sunset: Jews begin the Sabbath and festivals at sundown, Muslims pray Maghrib just after sunset, Christian monasteries pray vespers, and Hindus keep twilight prayers called sandhya.

screen: `DAY ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: silence. Your line: quiet is where it is. Which stretch of the day did you leave unfilled? What was it like in there? Day eleven.
screen: `SILENCE.` → `QUIET IS WHERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: Go outside at sunset and watch what happens to people. Someone on a balcony stops scrolling and just looks. Someone pulls over to take a photo of a sky they've seen a thousand times. The light goes gold, then orange, then that strange blue, and even busy people slow down for a second. In place after place, people have treated the end of the day as a doorway, and walked through it on purpose. This path lives at that hour. Today's word is the sun, and why its going down matters so much.
screen: `THE LIGHT GOES GOLD.` → `EVEN BUSY PEOPLE SLOW DOWN.` → `THE END OF THE DAY IS A DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: Start with how the Hebrew Bible counts a day. In Genesis, after each day of creation, the King James wording says: "And the evening and the morning were the first day." Evening first. Jewish tradition reads the day that way: the Sabbath and the festivals begin at sundown, with candles lit as the light goes. In Islam, one of the five daily prayers, called Maghrib, is prayed just after the sun sets, and during Ramadan, sunset is the moment the day's fast is broken, often with a date and water. In Christian monasteries, the evening prayer is called vespers, the Latin word for evening, and Anglican churches sing evensong. A Psalm sung at evening prayer asks that "the lifting up of my hands" be "as the evening sacrifice." In Hindu tradition, the twilights are called sandhya, the joinings, where night meets day and day meets night, and the prayers said at those hinges carry the same name. Each home has its own prayer and its own reason for it. Why sunset? Part of it is the body. Falling light is one of the signals your body uses to start winding toward sleep. Part of it is work: without lamps, when the light went, so did the working day. And part of it is simply that sunset is a bell nobody has to ring. It comes every day, for free. A doorway that opens by itself. The traditions just asked people to walk through it.
screen: `EVENING FIRST, THEN MORNING.` · `MAGHRIB, AND THE FAST BROKEN.` · `VESPERS AND THE JOININGS.` · `A BELL NOBODY HAS TO RING.` · then, large: `A DOORWAY THAT OPENS BY ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Wherever you are, find the light. A window, a lamp, the glow of the screen if that's all there is. Look at it for a breath. Then close your eyes and sit for about forty-five seconds, and let the day behind you be finished. Whatever didn't get done can wait for tomorrow's light. You're in the doorway now. The bell holds the time.
The sun. And its going down: a doorway that Jews, Muslims, Christians and Hindus each walk through in their own way. Eleventh word.
screen: `THE SUN — your 11th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: stop when the light does. Tonight, catch the moment the light changes, and stop for one breath. Just one. Let it close the day. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RAM DASS: WE'RE ALL JUST WALKING EACH OTHER HOME.`

12.title: Ram Dass: we're all just walking each other home
12.hook: Ram Dass: we're all just walking each other home
12.tomorrow: do something for someone with no receipt
12.howItsDone: Walking is practiced in many traditions: pilgrims walk to holy places, Muslims walk around the Kaaba during Hajj and Umrah, and Zen monks do slow walking meditation, called kinhin, between periods of sitting.

screen: `DAY TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: the sun. Your line: stop when the light does. Did you catch the light changing last night, and stop for one breath? Day twelve.
screen: `THE SUN.` → `STOP WHEN THE LIGHT DOES.`

segments.voice: Remember being walked home. Maybe after a party, maybe as a kid after dark, maybe after a bad day when a friend said, come on, I'll walk with you. They didn't fix anything. They didn't have a speech. They just went the same way you were going, for a while, so you didn't have to go alone. In the 1960s a Harvard psychologist named Richard Alpert went to India, met a teacher, and came back with a new name: Ram Dass. His best-known saying is the one in today's title. Today's word is walking.
screen: `SOMEONE WALKED YOU HOME.` → `THEY DIDN'T FIX ANYTHING.` → `A HARVARD PSYCHOLOGIST GOES TO INDIA.`

segments.voice: Ram Dass taught for more than fifty years, and he said the line in many ways: that underneath everything, all any of us are doing is keeping each other company on the way home. Home can mean different things depending on who's listening: God, death, the true self, or simply the end of the road. He left that open, on purpose. What's striking is how often the old paths chose walking as their picture. Pilgrims have walked for centuries: Christians along the roads to Santiago in Spain, Hindus to holy rivers, and Muslims at the Hajj walk seven times around the Kaaba and back and forth between two hills, retracing the steps of Hagar searching for water. In Zen monasteries, between long periods of sitting, monks rise and walk slowly in a line, a practice called kinhin, so that the stillness goes with them onto their feet. And in 1862, the American writer Henry David Thoreau published an essay simply called Walking. He wrote that he had met only one or two people in his life "who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering." He even claimed saunterer came from people wandering to the Holy Land, the Sainte Terre. Word scholars doubt it, and Thoreau may have known that. He liked the idea too much to let it go. Put them together and you get this: walking is how humans have practiced being on the way. Not arrived. On the way. And Ram Dass's twist is that you're never on it alone. The best thing you can do for anyone on the road is not to drag them or carry them. It's to walk beside them for a while.
screen: `KEEPING EACH OTHER COMPANY.` · `PILGRIMS ON THE ROAD.` · `KINHIN: STILLNESS ON YOUR FEET.` · `A GENIUS FOR SAUNTERING.` · then, large: `WALK BESIDE THEM FOR A WHILE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then bring to mind someone who is going through something right now. You don't have to fix it. For the next forty-five seconds, just picture yourself walking beside them. Same pace. No speech. Their side of the sidewalk and yours. If you pray, you can hold them in that. If you don't, just keep them company. The bell holds the time.
Walking. Being on the way, not arrived, and not alone. Twelfth word.
screen: `WALKING — your 12th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: walk someone home. Today, literally or not: walk with a friend to the car, or send the person you pictured a short message that says I'm here. Same pace. No fixing. Day twelve.

screen: `DAY 12 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DO SOMETHING FOR SOMEONE WITH NO RECEIPT.`

13.title: do something for someone with no receipt
13.hook: do something for someone with no receipt
13.tomorrow: you get one life and it ends
13.howItsDone: Sikhs volunteer in the langar, the free kitchen of the gurdwara; Jewish and Christian teaching both honor giving that the receiver, or the giver's own circle, never hears about; and Hindu teaching speaks of acting without attachment to reward.

screen: `DAY THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: walking. Your line: walk someone home. Who did you keep company, even by a message? Day thirteen.
screen: `WALKING.` → `WALK SOMEONE HOME.`

segments.voice: A good deed can come with a little receipt attached. I drove them to the airport. I remembered her birthday. I did the dishes, again. The receipts tend to print themselves. And sometimes the receipt wants to be seen: a thank-you, a mention, a like. Today is a small experiment against that. Do something for someone, and make sure there's no receipt: no thanks, no credit, maybe nobody even knowing it was you. Four traditions have a lot to say about that kind of giving. Today's word is service.
screen: `THE RECEIPT PRINTS ITSELF.` → `A THANK-YOU, A MENTION, A LIKE.` → `NO RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus talks about giving to the poor, and says to do it so quietly that, in the King James wording, you "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." Your own other hand shouldn't find out. The Jewish scholar Maimonides set out eight levels of giving, from grudging to generous. Near the very top: the giver and the receiver don't know each other's names. And at the top itself: helping someone so they won't need help again, with a gift, a loan, a partnership, a job. In Sikh tradition the word is seva, selfless service, and you can see it in the gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship. Gurdwaras keep a langar, a free kitchen where anyone, of any faith or none, sits and eats together. Volunteers cook, serve and wash up. At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the kitchen feeds a vast number of people every day, by volunteers whose names the people eating will never learn. And the Bhagavad Gita, in Hindu tradition, teaches acting without clinging to the fruits of the action: do the work well, and let go of what it earns you. The reasons differ. In Matthew, the Father sees what's done in secret. For Maimonides, the poor person's dignity matters. In the Gita, the doer lets go of the reward. They don't mean the same thing by it. But each of them treats the receipt as the part to throw away.
screen: `LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.` · `MAIMONIDES' LADDER OF GIVING.` · `SEVA AND THE FREE KITCHEN.` · `LET GO OF THE FRUITS.` · then, large: `THROW AWAY THE RECEIPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For the next forty-five seconds, think of one small thing you could do today for someone, where nobody would know it was you. Put a shopping cart back. Refill the coffee. Leave a kind review. Pay for something quietly. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it and walking away, no thank-you. Notice what that feels like. The bell holds the time.
Service. Doing good for someone else, without keeping the receipt. Thirteenth word.
screen: `SERVICE — your 13th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: no receipt. Today, do the thing you picked. Then don't mention it. Not to them, not to anyone. Tomorrow's the end of week two. Day thirteen.

14.howItsDone: Reflecting on death is an old practice: Stoics reminded themselves of it in their writings, Buddhists practice maranasati (mindfulness of death), and Christian art used the memento mori, a skull or hourglass, as a reminder.

segments.voice: Napkin math. Eighty years, times fifty-two weeks a year: a little over four thousand weeks. Four thousand. It sounds like a lot until you count the ones already gone. It's easy to live as if there's an endless supply, as if the big things, the call, the trip, the apology, can always wait for next month. Some traditions keep a practice for gently breaking that spell. A Roman emperor made a habit of it in his notebook. Today's word is the finite: you get one life, and it ends.
screen: `ABOUT FOUR THOUSAND WEEKS.` → `AS IF THERE'S AN ENDLESS SUPPLY.` → `ONE LIFE, AND IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: Marcus Aurelius, the emperor with the private notebook we met on day nine, reminded himself about death again and again. In George Long's translation: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good." Notice where the sentence lands. Not on fear. On be good, while you can. Today's line is memento mori, Latin for remember that you will die. Now, a small honesty. The popular story says the Stoics wrote it on their walls. There's no evidence they did. The Latin phrase is better known from later Christian art, from skulls and hourglasses on paintings and gravestones. The Stoics wrote the idea in their notebooks and letters rather than on plaster, and Marcus wrote his in Greek. And the idea isn't owned by any one school. The Psalms ask: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Early Buddhist texts teach maranasati, mindfulness of death, as a regular practice, not to frighten, but to wake up. A psalmist, the Buddha's early discourses, a Stoic emperor: very different hopes about what comes after. Each, in their own words, puts the end in view so the middle comes clear. And that's week two. Kindness, starting with yourself. Gratitude, said badly. Silence. The sun going down. Walking beside someone. Service with no receipt. And the finite, which gives all the others their weight. Seven more words, fourteen on your strand.
screen: `DEATH HANGS OVER THEE. BE GOOD.` · `LATER THAN THE STOICS.` · `NUMBER OUR DAYS.` · `WEEK TWO: SEVEN MORE WORDS.` · then, large: `REMEMBERING THE END CLEARS THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. It isn't meant to be heavy. Sit, and let the breath settle. For the next forty-five seconds, simply notice that this breath is one of a limited number. Not as a threat. Just as a fact. Then ask: if today counted, what's one small thing I'd want to do before it ends? A call, a thank-you, five minutes outside. Let the answer arrive. The bell holds the time.
The finite. You get one life, and it ends, and that's exactly what makes today count. Fourteenth word, and the end of week two.
